Title: Modular Sensory Stream for Integrating Physical Feedback in Vision-Language-Action Models
Text:
Modular Sensory Stream for Integrating Physical Feedback
in Vision-Language-Action Models
Jimin Lee 1 Huiwon Jang 1 2 Myungkyu Koo 1 2 Jungwoo Park 3 Jinwoo Shin 1 2
Abstract
Humans understand and interact with the real
world by relying on diverse physical feedback be-
yond visual perception. Motivated by this, recent
approaches attempt to incorporate physical sen-
sory signals into Vision-Language-Action mod-
els (VLAs). However, they typically focus on a
single type of physical signal, failing to capture
the heterogeneous and complementary nature of
real-world interactions. In this paper, we propose
MoSS, a modular sensory stream framework that
adapts VLAs to leverage multiple sensory signals
for action prediction. Specifically, we introduce
decoupled modality streams that integrate hetero-
geneous physical signals into the action stream
via joint cross-modal self-attention. To enable sta-
ble incorporation of new modalities, we adopt a
two-stage training scheme that freezes pretrained
VLA parameters in the early stage. Furthermore,
to better capture contact interaction dynamics, we
incorporate an auxiliary task that predicts future
physical signals. Through extensive real-world
experiments, we demonstrate that MoSS success-
fully augments VLAs to leverage diverse physical
signals (i.e., tactile and torque), integrating mul-
tiple signals to achieve synergistic performance
gains. The project page is available.
1. Introduction
In the real world, humans perform dexterous manipulation
by continuously integrating multiple sources of physical
sensory feedback that cannot be obtained through visual
perception alone. For example, during plug insertion, tactile
feedback at the fingertips helps recognize grasp stability,
while torque feedback from the arm provides crucial cues
for detecting contact and correcting misalignment.

Toward learning human-like generalizable policies, Vision-
Language-Action models (VLAs; Zitkovich et al. 2023;
Kim et al. 2024; Black et al. 2025a; Huang et al. 2025a;
Chen et al. 2025b; Bjorck et al. 2025a; Zheng et al. 2025)
have demonstrated remarkable progress by leveraging large-
scale pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs; Beyer
et al. 2024; Bai et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025a). However,
they rely solely on visual observations to generate actions,
which fundamentally limits their ability to handle precise
and contact-rich manipulation.
To mitigate this limitation, recent approaches have ex-
plored incorporating a single physical sensory modality
into pretrained VLAs, either by encoding it into VLM back-
bones (Zhang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2025b; Cheng
et al., 2025) or by directly conditioning the action expert
modules (Yu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). While effec-
tive in specific settings, such approaches are not designed to
grow with increasing sensory complexity; na¨ıvely extend-
ing them to incorporate multiple physical modalities does
not consistently yield complementary performance gains in
practice (see Figure 1). This highlights the need for a more
general and scalable framework that can effectively inte-
grate heterogeneous physical signals for reliable dexterous
manipulation.
Our approach.
We present MoSS, a Modular Sensory
Stream framework that seamlessly augments pretrained
VLAs to leverage diverse physical sensory signals for ac-
tion prediction. Specifically, we append decoupled modality
streams to the action expert module, which processes phys-
ical inputs and exchanges information with the pretrained
parameters via a joint cross-modal self-attention mechanism.
To avoid corruption of pretrained parameters by the newly
added streams, we introduce a two-stage training scheme.
In the first stage, we freeze the pretrained VLA and train
only the physical signal streams, allowing them to pre-align
their representations with the existing representation space
of the pretrained policy. After that, we jointly fine-tune the
entire model end-to-end. Furthermore, motivated by Zhang
et al. (2025b), we incorporate an auxiliary objective of fu-
ture physical signal prediction, which encourages the model
to internalize physical interaction dynamics and effectively
utilize physical feedback for action generation.

To validate the effectiveness of MoSS, we evaluate our
method on contact-rich, real-world manipulation tasks that
require physical interaction with surrounding environments
for precise control. We show that MoSS consistently im-
proves the performance of pretrained VLAs by effectively
leveraging physical feedback from both end-effector sensing
(i.e., tactile) and joint-level sensing (i.e., torque), compared
to other baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MoSS
can jointly incorporate multiple physical signals within a
single model, achieving cumulative performance gains by
combining complementary signals. To the best of our knowl-
edge, we are the first to present a unified VLA framework
that simultaneously exploits multiple physical signals.
We summarize the main contributions of this paper below:
• We propose MoSS, a modular framework that seamlessly
augments pretrained VLAs to leverage physical sensory
signals via decoupled modality streams and joint cross-
modal attention mechanisms.
• We introduce a two-stage training scheme with an auxil-
iary objective of future physical signal prediction, which
preserves pretrained VLA priors while ensuring effective
utilization of newly added modalities.
• We design contact-rich, real-world manipulation tasks
with diverse physical feedback (i.e., tactile and torque)
and show that MoSS achieves consistent and cumulative
performance gains over the baselines.
2. Related Works
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs).
The develop-
ment of generalist robot policies has been fundamentally
shaped by the challenge of acquiring diverse, large-scale
robotic datasets. While traditional approaches (Shafiul-
lah et al., 2022; Chi et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024) relied
on task-specific demonstrations with limited generaliza-
tion, VLAs address this bottleneck by leveraging pretrained
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for robotic control. Early
VLAs (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024) gener-
ate discretized actions autoregressively as tokens, while
more recent work (Black et al., 2025a; Bjorck et al., 2025a)
has shifted toward hybrid architectures in which diffusion-
based action heads are conditioned on VLM representations.
Despite these advances, current VLAs predominantly rely
on visual and linguistic modalities, overlooking physical
feedback (e.g., tactile, force, and torque) that is critical
for contact-rich manipulation. In this work, we focus on
diffusion-based VLAs and demonstrate how our approach
enables seamless integration of diverse physical sensory
signals into their action generation process.
Policy learning with physical feedback.
Recently, sev-
eral approaches have attempted to extend pretrained VLAs
with additional physical sensory modalities, demonstrat-
ing their effectiveness on contact-rich manipulation tasks.
Such physical signals can be broadly categorized into two
types based on their measurement location: (a) end-effector
sensing (e.g., tactile or force), and (b) joint-level sensing
(e.g., torque). For end-effector sensing, Yu et al. (2025);
Huang et al. (2025b); Bi et al. (2025); Cheng et al. (2025);
Adeniji et al. (2025) leverage external tactile or force sen-
sors mounted on the gripper or hand, while Zhang et al.
(2025a) employs high-resolution visuo-tactile sensors to
support tasks such as insertion, grasping, and fabric ma-
nipulation. For joint-level sensing, Zhang et al. (2025b)
utilizes torque feedback from arm joints to enable com-
pliant and contact-aware control. While these specialized
approaches demonstrate strong task-specific performance,
they typically focus on a single sensing modality. More-
over, recent attempts to integrate physical feedback with
vision and language (Cheng et al., 2025) often require com-

our framework provides a unified approach to incorporate

generalist policies that can flexibly leverage available physi-

Multimodal architectures.
Many recent efforts have at-
tempted to design an architecture to incorporate a diverse
range of modalities. In particular, the success of VLMs
has been largely driven by advances in multimodal fusion
architectures: early approaches (Nagrani et al., 2021; Wei
et al., 2020) employed cross-attention mechanisms to align
visual and textual representations, while more recent work
has explored richer fusion strategies, including perceiver-
based architectures (Jaegle et al., 2021), modality-specific
adapters (Li et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024), and unified
tokenization schemes (Lu et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2024;
Liang et al., 2024). These methods demonstrate that care-
fully designed fusion mechanisms can effectively model
heterogeneous modalities with different dimensionalities
and semantic structures. In the robotics domain, recent
VLAs (Black et al., 2025b; Bjorck et al., 2025b) have suc-
cessfully adapted such vision-language fusion techniques
to incorporate action prediction. However, extending these
architectures to physical sensing modalities poses additional
challenges, as such signals differ fundamentally from visual
and linguistic inputs in temporal structure, scale, and seman-
tics. Our work draws inspiration from multimodal fusion
in VLMs, but adapts it specifically to the action prediction
setting, introducing a modular architecture that enables pre-
trained VLAs to integrate diverse physical sensory signals
while preserving their action priors.

that augments pretrained Vision-Language-Action models
(VLAs) with physical sensory modalities. Formally, let ℓ

with its Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone Fθ to
obtain a unified visual-language representation ht:

Here, our goal is to augment such VLAs to leverage a

3.2. Two-Stage Training Strategy
We employ a two-stage training scheme designed to preserve
pretrained knowledge while enabling effective learning of
physical sensory representations.
Stage 1: Physical alignment.
We freeze all parameters of
the pretrained action expert module Aψ and train only the
modular sensory streams {Aϕi}N
i=1, which are initialized
from scratch. This allows the new streams to learn mean-
ingful representations of physical interactions (e.g., tactile
contacts, force feedback, and joint torques) and establish
cross-modal correspondences through joint self-attention,
without disrupting the pretrained action policy.
Stage 2: Joint fine-tuning.
After initializing the modular
sensory streams {Aϕi}N
i=1, we unfreeze the action expert
module Aψ and perform joint fine-tuning. This enables the
action stream to incorporate physical feedback M while
the sensory streams adapt to task-specific requirements,
allowing both streams to learn coordinated behaviors for
physically-aware manipulation. We find this staged train-
ing crucial for stability, as directly performing end-to-end
training from scratch leads to optimization difficulties due
to gradient interference between the randomly initialized
sensory streams {Aϕi}N
i=1 and pretrained action stream Aψ
(see Section 4.3).

4. Experiments
We investigate the following questions through experiments:
• Does applying MoSS to existing Vision-Language-Action
models (VLAs) effectively augment the base policy with
diverse physical feedback for contact-rich manipulation,
outperforming prior modality-augmented VLA baselines?
(Table 1 and Figure 4)
• Can MoSS scalably integrate multiple physical sensing
signals, enabling complementary effects across modali-
ties? (Table 1)
• How do individual components affect performance? (Ta-
ble 2 and Figures 5 and 6)
4.1. Experimental Setups
Tasks.
We evaluate MoSS on real-world, contact-rich ma-
nipulation tasks where interaction with physical feedback
(e.g., tactile on the end-effector and torque on arm joints)
is crucial for successful execution. Specifically, we design
the following tasks (see Figure 4 for the visualization of the
tasks, and see Appendix A.1 for more detailed descriptions):
• Unstack Cup. A robot should remove only the top red
cup from a stack of 3 inverted cups on the table. This
task requires regulating grasping force, as gripping too
strongly causes multiple cups to be lifted together.
• PnP Egg. A robot must pick up a fragile egg and place
it in a bowl without breaking it. This task requires fine-
grained feedback on end-effector to avoid excessive force.

A robot must erase a marked region on
a whiteboard using an eraser. This task requires sensing

• Plug Insertion. A robot must insert a plug into a socket,
which is often occluded from the (wrist-mounted) camera
view. This task requires torque and force cues to detect
contact and guide its alignment.
Hardware setup.
We construct a single-arm gripper plat-
form, which consists of a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 robotic
arm equipped with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, following the
DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) setup. Here, we mount an
AnySkin (Bhirangi et al., 2025) tactile sensor on the gripper,
while the robot arm itself supports torque sensing at each
joint. Specifically, for tactile signals, each AnySkin sensor
provides a 15-dimensional feature vector, obtained from
five sensing units that each measure a 3-dimensional force
vector (i.e., x, y, z). Since we attach one AnySkin sensor
to each gripper finger, our tactile sensing system provides a
30-dimensional observation vector at each timestep. For the
torque signals, the robot provides a 7-dimensional vector
(one scalar torque value per joint) measured in Newton-
meters. Further specifications of the physical sensory signal,
are provided in Appendix A.2.
Baselines.
To demonstrate the generality of our approach,
we apply MoSS to two state-of-the-art VLAs: π0 (Black
et al., 2025b) and GR00T N1.5 (Bjorck et al., 2025a). We
then compare MoSS with several modality-augmented VLA
baselines: (i) Tactile-VLA (Huang et al., 2025b) incorpo-
rates tactile signals on the gripper as additional input tokens
to the VLM backbone; (ii) ForceVLA (Yu et al., 2025) em-
ploys an MoE-based encoder to fuse 3-axis force signals on
the gripper with VLM features and conditions the action
expert module on them; (iii) TA-VLA (Zhang et al., 2025b)
injects torque signals from robotic arm joints directly into
the action expert module, while training the policy to predict
future torque signals as an auxiliary task. For each method,
we adapt it to use the physical sensory signals available on
our hardware platforms.
Implementation details.
For π0 and GR00T N1.5, we
follow the official implementation that performs full-fine-
tuning for π0, but we freeze the Vision-Language-Model
(VLM) backbone for GR00T N1.5. However, when extend-
ing GR00T N1.5 with Tactile-VLA, we also fine-tune the
VLM, as Tactile-VLA integrates tactile signals directly into
the VLM, requiring the backbone to adapt to this unseen
modality introduced during training. We train all models
on a consolidated dataset that combines the training data

4.2. Main Results
We provide quantitative results in Table 1, and the quali-
tative results of rollout examples in Figure 4. We provide
more results, including evaluation on simulated manipula-
tion benchmarks, in Section C.
In Table 1, we first observe that base VLAs (i.e., fine-
tuned VLAs without physical sensing) struggle on these
precision manipulation tasks, achieving average success
rates of 20.8% and 26.1% for GR00T N1.5 and π0, respec-
tively. This indicates that our tasks require fine-grained
force control, highlighting the difficulty of performing them
successfully with vision-and-language-only policies. This
confirms our hypothesis that vision and language alone are
insufficient for tasks requiring fine-grained force control.
In contrast, we find that our framework, MoSS, achieves
substantial improvements across all tasks and base mod-
els. For example, for GR00T N1.5, we achieve an average
improvement of 28.2% over the base model, with partic-
ularly strong gains on Unstack Cup (+37.5%) and Board
Erase (+29.2%). Similar improvements are observed on π0,
demonstrating that our approach generalizes across different
VLA architectures. We also find that MoSS consistently out-
performs several physical modality-augmented VLA base-
lines. For example, on the PnP Egg task, GR00T N1.5
+ MoSS with tactile signals achieves 66.7%, but GR00T
N1.5 + ForceVLA gets 54.2%. This highlights our design
that maintains a separate processing stream with controlled
cross-modal joint self-attention, which enables effective
integration of physical sensing without corrupting action
representation. Moreover, MoSS consistently improves as
we add additional physical sensor modalities, demonstrat-
ing that MoSS is scalable framework to adapt VLAs with
multiple physical modalities.
4.3. Analysis and Ablation Study
When does the VLA attend to physical feedback?
To
investigate when the VLA attends to physical feedback, we
visualize the attention patterns in our cross-modal attention
mechanism while performing the task. In Figure 5, we ob-
serve that action tokens attend strongly to torque and tactile
tokens when the generated actions require accurate, contact-
intensive control (e.g., when grasping softly), enabling the
model to modulate insertion or grasping force based on re-
sistance feedback. Notably, this demonstrates that MoSS
truly leverages physical sensory signals when generating
actions at moments that require accurate, contact-intensive
control.
Effect of decoupled multimodal stream architecture.
We investigate the effect of the separated multimodal stream
architecture. To evaluate this, we compare MoSS (i.e., de-
coupled multimodal stream design for the action expert),
against a na¨ıve Diffusion Transformer (DiT) action expert
that jointly predicts physical sensory signals within a single
stream. In Table 2, we observe that our decoupled multi-
modal architecture significantly outperforms the DiT action
expert. For example, on the Unstack Cup task, it achieves
20.9% improvements over the na¨ıve DiT baseline. These re-
sults indicate that decoupling distinct modalities to separate
streams is crucial for effectively adapting VLAs to diverse
physical sensory signals.

Effect of two-stage training.
We also investigate the ef-
fect of our two-stage training scheme. To evaluate this,
we compare MoSS trained with either single or two-stage

the VLA without freezing pretrained parameters. As shown
in Table 2, we find that a two-stage training scheme is criti-

modalities, e.g., on the Unstack Cup task, it yields a 16.7%
improvement over single-stage training.
Effect of future physical modality prediction.
Figure 6
visualizes how MoSS predicts future physical sensory sig-

physical modality prediction objective. In Figure 6, we eval-
uate prediction dynamics during contact transitions. We find
that MoSS generates actions by predicting tactile signals;
for instance, MoSS anticipates contact by predicting rising
tactile signals, which prompts increased gripping force.
In Table 2, we investigate the effect of our future physical
modality prediction objective. To evaluate this, we compare
MoSS trained with and without the future prediction objec-
tive. We find that the future prediction objective provides
meaningful guidance that helps the model generate more
accurate actions. For instance, on the Unstack Cup task, the
prediction objective improves performance by 8.4% (45.8
→54.2%).
Inference efficiency.
MoSS introduces additional process-
ing for multiple physical sensory signals. Then, how does
this extension affect inference latency? In Table 3, we an-
alyze the inference latency of GR00T N1.5 + MoSS when
incorporating multiple signals. We find that when both
tactile and torque modalities are incorporated, latency in-
creases by only 2.4 ms (1.11× slower than the base model),
highlighting the efficiency of MoSS. Importantly, MoSS of-
fers significant performance gain in real-world tasks while
incurring only a marginal increase in inference latency.
5. Conclusion
In this work, we have presented MoSS, a scalable modu-
lar framework that adapts Vision-Language-Action models
(VLAs) to leverage multiple sensory signals for action pre-
diction. By extending the action experts with new streams,
MoSS can incorporate various modalities without corrupting
the pretrained features. Our experiments show that MoSS
improves performance on contact-rich, real-world manipu-
lation tasks, and the performance continues to improve as
more physical sensory modalities are incorporated. We hope
our approach facilitates future research toward generalist
robot policies that can leverage a diverse range of physical
sensory modalities.

Impact Statement
This paper presents a framework for general robotics foun-
dation models. Thus, there is a risk of potential misuse of
our model for malicious purposes, e.g., unauthorized actions
that cause physical harm, property damage, or safety viola-
tions. To mitigate such risks, we encourage deployments to
restrict our model to controlled environments, to integrate
hardware-level safety components (e.g., force limits), and
to require human supervision for all high-risk tasks.

A. Experimental Details
A.1. Task Specifications.
We collected 100 datasets per task with extensive variation across multiple dimensions to ensure robust generalization and
avoid memorization. We use the third-person view camera and wrist camera of 720×1280 resolution without depth. We use
the visual observation after resizing it to 224×224 resolution. We use absolute joint position as action mode. We describe
the detailed scenarios as follows:
Unstack Cup: The task required lifting only the top red cup from a stack. To prevent gripper position memorization, we
varied the cup sizes, using both large and small cups in different configurations. In particular, we evaluate each model over
24 trials, consisting of 12 trials with a large cup and 12 trials with a small cup. We use the instruction “Pick up the top red
cup from the stack and place it next to the blue cup.” for this task.
PnP Egg: The egg was placed in various positions across the workspace to evaluate spatial generalization. We evaluate each
model over 24 trials. We use the instruction “Pick up the egg and place it in the gold bowl.” for this task.
Board Erase: The whiteboard was positioned at three different heights to test height adaptability. We varied the eraser
colors (red and grey) with slight differences in object size, and used markers of different colors (blue and black). Evaluations
were conducted across diverse environmental conditions to assess robustness. In particular, we evaluate each model over 24
trials, consisting of one trial per combination of (height, eraser color, object size, different color). We use the instruction
“Use the (red/grey) eraser to clean the whiteboard.” for this task.
Plug Insertion: We used chargers of three different colors (yellow, black, and white) for color and object generalization,
with target insertion positions varied across trials. We evaluate each model over 24 trials, consisting of 8 trials per charger.
We use the instruction “Pick up the (yellow/white/black) charger and plug it into the socket.” for this task.

B.2. Failure Case Analysis
While MoSS demonstrates meaningful improvement on contact-rich tasks, we find several failure cases, which are visualized
in Figure 8. First, in tasks such as Unstack Cup, PnP Egg, and Board Erase, we observe that when the base policy fails to
reach the target object or establish a stable grasp, MoSS cannot compensate. This is because the physical feedback never
becomes informative at these stages, since the gripper has not yet made meaningful contact. Moreover, in the Plug Insertion
task, we observe that when the initial grasp is imperfect, it results in a misaligned plug angle that prevents successful
socket insertion. As with the first case, this is also related to the grasping quality issue that occurs before physical feedback
becomes effective.

Abstract: Humans understand and interact with the real world by relying on diverse physical feedback be- yond visual perception. Motivated by this, recent approaches attempt to incorporate physical sen- sory signals into Vision-Language-Action mod- els (VLAs). However, they typically focus on a single type of physical signal, failing to capture the heterogeneous and complementary nature of real-world interactions. In this paper, we propose MoSS, a modular sensory stream framework that adapts VLAs to leverage multiple sensory signals for action prediction. Specifically, we introduce decoupled modality streams that integrate hetero- geneous physical signals into the action stream via joint cross-modal self-attention. To enable sta- ble incorporation of new modalities, we adopt a two-stage training scheme that freezes pretrained VLA parameters in the early stage. Furthermore, to better capture contact interaction dynamics, we incorporate an auxiliary task that predicts future physical signals. Through extensive real-world experiments, we demonstrate that MoSS success- fully augments VLAs to leverage diverse physical signals (i.e., tactile and torque), integrating mul- tiple signals to achieve synergistic performance gains.
